notes.title: ICT Forex - Considerations In Risk Management
notes.own:
Considerations in Risk Management

The main point is that survival comes before profit.

It does not matter how good my entries are if I risk too much and eventually lose the account. Losing streaks are unavoidable, and at some point I need to be prepared for eight or more losses in a row.

The goal is not to create a system that never loses.

The goal is to make sure that a losing streak cannot remove me from the game.

Why Large Risk Does Not Work

Risking 10% on each trade is completely unsustainable.

A few winning trades may make it feel like it works, but an eight-trade losing streak would reduce a $10,000 account to approximately $4,305. That is almost a 57% drawdown.

Risking 5% is still far too aggressive. Eight consecutive losses would reduce the same account to approximately $6,634, which is almost a 34% drawdown.

Once my drawdown becomes that large, I am unlikely to trade normally. I may start:

Forcing trades
Increasing size
Holding losing positions
Ignoring invalidation
Revenge trading
Trying to recover everything immediately
Fighting the market because I need to be right

That is how a normal losing period turns into a blown account.

Mental Capital

My account balance is not necessarily the same as the amount I am mentally prepared to lose.

I may technically have $10,000 in the account, but if losing $4,000 would completely affect my confidence and decision-making, then I am not really trading with $10,000 in mental capital.

Risk needs to be small enough that one normal loss does not change how I approach the next setup.

If one loss makes me emotional, desperate or unable to sleep, I am risking too much.

Losses Are Part of Trading

I will have losses regardless of how good my strategy is.

There is no method that can give me perfect accuracy. Even a profitable trader can experience a long sequence of losses.

The question is not:

How do I avoid every loss?

The better question is:

How do I control the damage when the losses arrive?

My risk management must be designed around the possibility that the next several trades may all lose.

My Risk Reduction Model

My maximum normal risk should be 2%.

After a loss, I immediately reduce the risk by half:

Normal risk: 2%
After the first loss: 1%
After another loss: 0.5%
If losses continue: remain at 0.5%
If necessary after several more losses: reduce again to 0.25%

The main rule is:

Every loss causes me to reduce risk, never increase it.

I should not double my risk because I want the money back. I should not average down or convince myself that the next trade has to win because the previous trades lost.

The market does not owe me a recovery trade.

Example: $10,000 Account

This is what happens if I begin with 2% risk, reduce to 1% after the first loss and then reduce to 0.5% after the second loss:

Trade	Risk rate	Amount lost	Balance
Starting balance	—	—	$10,000
Loss 1	2%	−$200	$9,800
Loss 2	1%	−$98	$9,702
Loss 3	0.5%	−$48.51	$9,653.49
Loss 4	0.5%	−$48.27	$9,605.22
Loss 5	0.5%	−$48.03	$9,557.20
Loss 6	0.5%	−$47.79	$9,509.41
Loss 7	0.5%	−$47.55	$9,461.86
Loss 8	0.5%	−$47.31	$9,414.55

After eight consecutive losses:

Remaining balance: approximately $9,414.55
Total drawdown: approximately $585.45
Percentage drawdown: approximately 5.85%

The exact calculation differs slightly from the rounded numbers used in the video, but the principle is the same.

What Happens If I Keep Risking 2%?

If I continue risking 2% after every loss:

Trade	Amount lost	Balance
Starting balance	—	$10,000
Loss 1	−$200	$9,800
Loss 2	−$196	$9,604
Loss 3	−$192.08	$9,411.92
Loss 4	−$188.24	$9,223.68
Loss 5	−$184.47	$9,039.21
Loss 6	−$180.78	$8,858.42
Loss 7	−$177.17	$8,681.26
Loss 8	−$173.63	$8,507.63

After eight consecutive losses:

Fixed 2% risk: approximately $1,492 lost
Reduced-risk model: approximately $585 lost
Capital protected by reducing risk: approximately $907

The model does not prevent losses. It prevents those losses from causing unnecessary damage.

Risk Comparison

This is what eight consecutive losses do to a $10,000 account:

Risk model	Balance after 8 losses	Drawdown
Fixed 10%	$4,304.67	56.95%
Fixed 5%	$6,634.20	33.66%
Fixed 2%	$8,507.63	14.92%
Reduced model	$9,414.55	5.85%

The size of my risk matters more than whether the next individual trade wins.

Why Reducing Risk Works

My risk becomes smaller when my execution is most uncertain.

If I am in a drawdown, I may be:

Reading the market poorly
Trading under the wrong conditions
Rushing my entries
Dealing with personal stress
Breaking my rules
Using a model that is temporarily underperforming

I may not know the exact reason immediately. Reducing risk gives me time to find it without causing serious damage.

I may not make much money while trading at 0.5%, but making money quickly is not the objective during a drawdown.

The objective is:

Protecting capital
Regaining discipline
Rebuilding confidence
Proving that my execution has stabilized
Remaining in the game
Recovering Back to Normal Risk

I should not return directly from 0.5% to 2%.

The increase must happen gradually.

From 0.5% Back to 1%

I remain at 0.5% risk until I recover at least 50% of the loss created while risking 1%.

For example, if the 1% loss was $100, I need to recover at least $50 while using 0.5% risk before returning to 1%.

From 1% Back to 2%

I remain at 1% risk until I recover at least 50% of the loss created while risking 2%.

If the 2% loss was $200, I need to recover at least $100 while using 1% risk before returning to 2%.

If I lose again during the recovery, I reduce my risk again.

The complete process is:

2% → loss → 1% → loss → 0.5% → recovery → 1% → recovery → 2%.

What I Should Never Do

After a loss, my first thought should not be:

How can I make this money back?

My first thought should be:

How can I reduce my exposure and protect the account?

I should never:

Increase size after a loss
Revenge trade
Average down on a losing position
Add more money to fix poor risk management
Force a larger target because I want to recover faster
Refuse to exit because I need to be right
Impose my will on the market
Trade normal size while stress is affecting my decisions

Adding more money is not the answer if the actual problem is poor risk control.

Applying This to My NQ Trading

For my prop accounts, percentages can be misleading.

A 50K prop account does not give me $50,000 of real loss capacity. My actual capital is the drawdown I am permitted before the account fails.

It therefore makes more sense to use a fixed-dollar version:

Normal risk: $200
After the first loss: $100
After another loss: $50
If losses continue: remain at $50
If necessary: reduce again to $25
Eight-Loss Example With My Risk
Trade	Risk	Result	Total drawdown
1	$200	−$200	−$200
2	$100	−$100	−$300
3	$50	−$50	−$350
4	$50	−$50	−$400
5	$50	−$50	−$450
6	$50	−$50	−$500
7	$50	−$50	−$550
8	$50	−$50	−$600

If I continued risking $200 on every trade:

Eight losses × $200 = $1,600 drawdown.

Using the reduced-risk model:

$200 + $100 + six $50 losses = $600 drawdown.

This protects $1,000 during the exact same losing streak.

Rebuilding My $200 Risk

After losing at the $100 tier, I remain at $50 risk until I recover at least $50.

After recovering that amount, I can return to $100 risk.

I then remain at $100 until I recover at least $100. Once that happens, I can return to my normal $200 risk.

Situation	My next risk
Normal trading	$200
First loss	$100
Second loss	$50
Continued losses	Remain at $50
Recover at least $50	$100
Recover at least $100 at the $100 tier	$200
Lose during recovery	Reduce again

The sequence is:

$200 → loss → $100 → loss → $50 → recovery → $100 → recovery → $200.

Recovery Example

After eight losses, I am down $600 and risking $50.

Assuming every winner produces 1R:

Trade	Risk	Result	Remaining drawdown	Next risk
After losing streak	$50	—	−$600	$50
Recovery win 1	$50	+$50	−$550	$100
Recovery win 2	$100	+$100	−$450	$200

I am still down $450 overall, but my execution has shown enough recovery to gradually return to normal risk.

The purpose is not to recover the complete drawdown before increasing risk. The purpose is to require proof that my performance is improving before I put normal size back on.

Main Takeaway

Risk management is more important than my entry model.

A good setup cannot protect me if I am overleveraged. My only real defense is controlling how much money I expose when I am wrong.

Without the model:

Poor performance + emotional pressure + normal risk = larger drawdown.

With the model:

Poor performance + reduced risk = controlled damage and time to recover.

So my rule is:

Losses are unavoidable. Large drawdowns are not. After a loss, I reduce risk. After another loss, I reduce it again. I remain small until my results prove that the recovery has started, and then I gradually return to normal size.

The objective is not to win the next trade.

The objective is to survive long enough for my edge to work over time.

* I then remain at $100 risk until I recover at least $100. Once that happens, I can return to my normal $200 risk.

| Situation | My Next Risk |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Normal trading** | $200 |
| **First loss** | $100 |
| **Second loss** | $50 |
| **Continued losses** | Remain at $50 |
| **Recover at least $50** | $100 |
| **Recover at least $100 at the $100 tier** | $200 |
| **Lose during recovery** | Reduce again |

* **Rebuilding Sequence**: $200 → loss → $100 → loss → $50 → recovery → $100 → recovery → $200.

### Recovery Example (Assumes 1R Winners)
*After eight losses, I am down $600 and risking $50:*

| Trade | Risk | Result | Remaining Drawdown | Next Risk |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **After losing streak** | $50 | — | -$600 | $50 |
| **Recovery win 1** | $50 | +$50 | -$550 | $100 |
| **Recovery win 2** | $100 | +$100 | -$450 | $200 |

* *Key Principle*: I am still down $450 overall, but my execution has shown enough recovery to gradually return to normal risk. The purpose is not to recover the complete drawdown before increasing risk; the purpose is to require proof that my performance is improving before I put normal size back on.

## Main Takeaway
* **Risk management is more important than my entry model**: A good setup cannot protect me if I am overleveraged. My only real defense is controlling how much money I expose when I am wrong.
* **Without the model**: Poor performance + emotional pressure + normal risk = larger drawdown.
* **With the model**: Poor performance + reduced risk = controlled damage and time to recover.
* **My Ultimate Rule**: Losses are unavoidable. Large drawdowns are not. After a loss, I reduce risk. After another loss, I reduce it again. I remain small until my results prove that the recovery has started, and then I gradually return to normal size.

> The objective is not to win the next trade. The objective is to survive long enough for my edge to work over time.
notes.summary: This lesson teaches a systematic risk reduction model designed to preserve both financial and mental capital during inevitable losing streaks. By automatically cutting risk in half after losses and only scaling back up gradually based on performance milestones, a trader can limit drawdown to single digits and ensure survival in the market.
rules: If I experience a loss at my normal risk tier, then I must immediately reduce my risk size by half on the next trade.
If I experience a second consecutive loss, then I must reduce my risk to the minimum tier (0.5% or $50) and keep it there until performance stabilizes.
If I am at a reduced risk tier, then I must recover at least 50% of the dollar loss from the previous tier before increasing my size back up.
If I experience a loss while attempting to step up my risk during recovery, then I must immediately reduce my risk back to the previous lower tier.
If I am in a drawdown, then I must never average down, revenge trade, or increase risk size to recover losses quickly.
core_ideas: Survival always comes before profit; excellent entry models are worthless if overleveraged risk destroys the account.
A losing streak cannot be allowed to remove me from the game or trigger a destructive psychological spiral.
My true trading capital is defined by my mental capital and permitted drawdown, not just the account balance.
Risk must be systematically reduced when execution is uncertain, and only scaled back up with proven performance.

notes.own_fmt:
## What New Traders Should Focus On

The main point is to look at price based on where orders and liquidity are resting instead of making the chart more complicated than it needs to be.

Everything starts with:
- Open
- High
- Low
- Close
- Time

The chart already gives me the information I need. My job is to train my eyes to understand what price is showing me and where other traders are likely positioned.

## Finding Liquidity

The easiest place to start is with equal highs and equal lows. Equal highs usually have buy stops resting above them because traders who are short will normally place their stop-losses above those highs. Equal lows usually have sell stops resting below them because traders who are long will normally place their stop-losses below those lows.

So:
- Equal highs = buy-side liquidity above.
- Equal lows = sell-side liquidity below.

They do not need to be perfectly equal. If they visually look close enough to form a double top or double bottom, I can treat them as a potential liquidity pool.

The main question I should ask is: Where will other traders’ ideas fail, and where are their stops likely resting?

I should not only think about where I want to enter. I need to think about where other traders have entered, where they will be forced out and whether their exit can create an opportunity for me.

## How I Should Look at Price

Retail traders may see equal lows as support and buy from them. They may see equal highs as resistance and sell from them.

I should look beyond the level itself. If traders are buying equal lows, their sell stops are likely resting below. If traders are selling equal highs, their buy stops are likely resting above.

Orders normally rest:
- Above old highs
- Above equal highs
- Below old lows
- Below equal lows

Price moves between these areas of liquidity. After liquidity on one side is taken, price may begin moving toward liquidity on the opposite side. That does not mean every liquidity raid will reverse. Taking liquidity is not automatically an entry signal. I still need context explaining why price should take the level and what it should do afterward.

## Building the Trade

The basic process is:
- Identify equal highs, equal lows, old highs or old lows.
- Mark where the buy stops and sell stops are resting.
- Determine which liquidity pool price is most likely targeting.
- Find an entry before price reaches that objective.
- Make sure there is enough room between my entry and target.
- Define where the idea becomes invalid.
- Scale profits as price moves toward the liquidity.

The liquidity pool gives me the objective. It does not give me the entire trade.

## OTE and Order Blocks

I can use an OTE retracement to refine my entry, but the Fibonacci itself is not what makes the trade work. The reason for the trade must come from the context and the liquidity objective. The Fibonacci only helps me find a better entry inside the retracement.

If I miss the original OTE, I should not automatically chase price. I can wait for price to retrace into a properly contextualized order block.

For a short, I can look at the up-close candle before the move lower. However, every up-close candle is not automatically a bearish order block. There must already be a reason for expecting price to move lower.

If sell stops are resting beneath equal lows and price is expected to attack them, a retracement to the low of the bearish order block may provide the short entry. If the short idea is valid, price should remain below the order block while moving toward the target. My stop should be placed beyond the level that invalidates the trade.

## Avoiding Chasing

Entering after price has started moving does not always mean that I am chasing. It becomes chasing when price has already moved too far toward the target and there is not enough profit potential remaining.

Before entering, I need to compare:
- Entry price
- Stop-loss and invalidation
- Liquidity target
- Remaining profit potential

I can be correct about direction and still take a bad trade if I enter too close to the target.

## Measuring the Raid

In Forex, liquidity may be taken by approximately 10–20 pips beyond the high or low, and sometimes more. I should not convert that directly into a fixed number of NQ points. NQ volatility changes based on the session, time and market conditions.

Instead, I need to study:
- How far NQ normally trades beyond equal highs and lows
- Whether the move happens during an important time window
- Whether price rejects or accepts beyond the level
- Whether displacement appears after the raid
- Where the next liquidity pool is located

The important thing is understanding that touching the exact high or low may not be enough. Price may need to trade properly through the level to trigger the stops resting beyond it.

## Managing the Trade

I do not need the final target to be reached for the trade to make money.

As price approaches the expected liquidity, I can:
- Take partial profits
- Reduce my initial risk
- Move the stop only when the trade has earned it
- Leave a smaller portion open for the deeper objective

This allows me to make money even if I am wrong about the full extension. I may correctly identify the liquidity raid but be wrong about how far price will continue. Scaling profits means the entire trade does not depend on one perfect target.

## Practice

My first job is to train my eyes, not force trades. I should choose one or two markets and repeatedly mark:
- Equal highs
- Equal lows
- Buy stops
- Sell stops
- Old highs and lows
- How far price trades beyond the level
- What price does after taking the liquidity
- The time of the raid
- The next liquidity objective

The 15-minute chart is a good place to begin, although these formations can appear on every timeframe because price is fractal. I should first annotate and observe without trying to predict every move. Once I practise executions, the goal should be quality and discipline rather than taking as many trades as possible.

## Main Takeaway

Equal highs and lows are not complete trade setups. They only show me where liquidity may be resting.

For an actual trade, I need:
- A clear liquidity pool
- A reason for price to target it
- A contextual entry
- Enough room to the objective
- Clear invalidation
- Proper risk management
- A plan for taking profits

So, in short: Find where traders are positioned, understand where their stops are resting and determine which liquidity pool price is likely moving toward. Use that liquidity as the objective, but wait for context and a valid entry before taking the trade.
notes.ai:
## The Core Philosophy: OHLC and Time

Everything on the chart starts with the basics: **Open, High, Low, Close, and Time** (OHLC+T). The chart already provides all the information I need; my job is simply to train my eyes to understand what price is showing me and where other traders are likely positioned. Instead of making the chart complicated, I must look at price based on where orders and liquidity are resting.

## Finding and Interpreting Liquidity

The easiest place to start mapping liquidity is by identifying **equal highs** and **equal lows**.
*   **Equal highs** = **Buy-side liquidity** resting above. Traders who are short will normally place their protective buy stops above these highs.
*   **Equal lows** = **Sell-side liquidity** resting below. Traders who are long will normally place their protective sell stops below these lows.

*Note on execution:* These levels do not need to be mathematically perfect. If they visually look close enough to form a **double top** or **double bottom**, I will treat them as a valid **liquidity pool**.

The key question I must constantly ask is: *Where will other traders’ ideas fail, and where are their stops likely resting?* I cannot just think about where I want to enter. I must think about where others entered, where they will be forced to exit, and how their forced exits create an opportunity for me.

## How to Look at Price (Retail vs. Institutional)

Retail traders look at equal lows as support (to buy) and equal highs as resistance (to sell). I must look beyond the level itself:
*   If retail is buying equal lows, their sell stops are building up below.
*   If retail is selling equal highs, their buy stops are building up above.

Price systematically moves between these areas of liquidity. Orders normally rest:
*   Above old highs / equal highs
*   Below old lows / equal lows

Once liquidity on one side is swept, price may begin moving toward liquidity on the opposite side. However, **taking liquidity is not automatically an entry signal**. A liquidity raid does not guarantee a reversal; I still need context explaining why price should take that level and what it should do afterward.

## The Trade Building Process

The basic process for building a trade is:
1.  **Identify** equal highs, equal lows, old highs, or old lows.
2.  **Mark** where the buy stops and sell stops are resting.
3.  **Determine** which liquidity pool price is most likely targeting (this pool gives me my objective, not the entire trade).
4.  **Find an entry** before price reaches that objective.
5.  **Check room**: Ensure there is enough distance between my entry and my target.
6.  **Define invalidation**: Establish exactly where the trade idea becomes invalid.
7.  **Scale profits** as price moves toward the liquidity.

## Entry Refinement: OTE and Order Blocks

*   **Optimal Trade Entry (OTE):** I can use an OTE Fibonacci retracement to refine my entry, but the Fibonacci itself is what makes the trade work. The actual reason for the trade must come from the context and the liquidity objective. The Fib simply helps me find a better entry price inside the retracement.
*   **Order Blocks:** If I miss the original OTE, I must not chase price. Instead, I can wait for price to retrace into a properly contextualized **order block**.
    *   For a short trade, I look at the up-close candle before the move lower.
    *   *Warning:* Every up-close candle is not automatically a bearish **order block**. There must already be a narrative/reason expecting price to move lower.
    *   If sell stops are resting beneath equal lows and price is expected to attack them, a retracement to the low of the bearish order block can provide my short entry.
    *   If the short setup is valid, price should remain below the order block while moving toward the target. My stop must be placed beyond the level that invalidates the trade.

## Avoiding Chasing and Managing Risk

*   **What is Chasing?** Entering after price has started moving is not always chasing. It officially becomes **chasing** when price has already moved too far toward the target, leaving insufficient profit potential relative to the required stop-loss.
*   Before entering, I must compare:
    *   Entry price
    *   Stop-loss / Invalidation level
    *   Liquidity target
    *   Remaining profit potential
*   Even if I am correct about direction, I will take a bad trade if I enter too close to the target.

## Measuring the Raid (Forex vs. Index Futures)

*   In Forex, liquidity is typically swept by approximately **10–20 pips** beyond the high or low (sometimes more).
*   **Do not convert this directly into a fixed number of NQ points.** NQ (Nasdaq) volatility changes dynamically based on the session, time, and market conditions.
*   Instead of using a fixed point value for NQ, I must study:
    *   How far NQ normally trades beyond equal highs/lows.
    *   Whether the move happens during an important time window.
    *   Whether price rejects or accepts the level.
    *   Whether **displacement** appears after the raid.
    *   Where the next liquidity pool is located.
*   *Key takeaway:* Simply touching the exact high or low is often not enough; price may need to trade properly through the level to trigger the resting stops.

## Trade Management: Getting Paid

I do not need price to hit my final target to make money. As price approaches the target liquidity, I can:
1.  Take partial profits.
2.  Reduce my initial risk.
3.  Move the stop only when the trade has earned it.
4.  Leave a smaller portion open for deeper objectives.

Scaling profits means the success of the trade does not depend on one perfect target. If I am correct about the raid but wrong about how far the continuation goes, I still walk away profitable.

## Practice and Eye Training Plan

My first job is to train my eyes, not to force executions. I will focus on one or two markets and repeatedly mark up:
*   Equal highs and equal lows (buy stops and sell stops).
*   Old highs and old lows.
*   How far price trades beyond these levels.
*   Price behavior immediately after taking liquidity.
*   The time of the raid.
*   The next liquidity objective.

The **15-minute chart** is the ideal place to start. Because price is fractal, these same formations appear on all timeframes. I should first annotate and observe without trying to predict every move. Once I practice actual executions, my goal must be quality and discipline rather than trade volume.
notes.summary: This lesson teaches new traders to stop overcomplicating charts and focus entirely on where orders and liquidity are resting. By identifying where retail stop-losses are clustered, traders can locate clear target objectives. True trading success comes from pairing these liquidity targets with institutional context, clean entries, and disciplined risk management.
rules: If equal highs or equal lows visually form a double top or bottom, then treat them as a valid liquidity pool even if they are not mathematically perfect.
If you miss the original OTE retracement, then do not chase price; wait for a retracement into a properly contextualized order block.
If you enter a short trade using a bearish order block, then price must remain below that block, and your stop must be placed beyond the invalidation level.
If price begins moving toward your liquidity objective, then take partial profits and reduce your initial risk instead of holding out for one perfect target.
core_ideas: Price moves systematically between areas of liquidity, targeting the stops of retail traders who are forced out of their positions.
Equal highs and equal lows are target objectives that give you the direction, not complete trade setups on their own.
Chasing occurs when you enter too close to your target, destroying your risk-to-reward ratio even if you are correct about direction.
You do not need price to reach your final target to make money; scaling partials ensures you get paid even if the move fails to fully extend.
